opus-5.5.text:
I think they're useful, but you have to be pretty careful about which part of the analogy you're leaning on.

The tempting move is to say that gradient descent is like evolution: a dumb outer optimization process producing a smart system that ends up wanting things the optimizer never "intended." Evolution selected for inclusive genetic fitness, and humans care about food, sex, status, art, and our kids, and then we invent contraception. So the worry goes: you train a model on some objective, and it develops internal goals that correlate with that objective in training but come apart once it's in a new situation. I think that's a real and important intuition pump. It shows that "the outer objective" and "what the resulting system actually wants" can be different things, and that selection pressure alone doesn't guarantee alignment.

But there are big disanalogies. Evolution is incredibly sample-inefficient and indirect. It doesn't see what's happening inside an organism and only gets feedback through reproduction, many generations removed from the behavior that mattered. With ML training, we choose the data. We give feedback on individual behaviors. We can look at the internals, at least in principle, and we can iterate quickly. So the gap between "what we're selecting for" and "what we get" doesn't have to be as large as it was for evolution. Saying "evolution failed to align humans, so we'll fail to align AI" overstates the case, in the same way that saying "it'll be fine because we're much more careful than evolution" understates it.

Human learning, meaning within-lifetime learning, is in some ways a closer analogy for what a single training run does. You have a learning algorithm, a lot of experience, and some reward signals, and out comes a system with fairly rich values that partly reflect those rewards and partly don't. People don't straightforwardly maximize dopamine. They form attachments to things, and their values are shaped by but not identical to their reinforcement history. That's relevant evidence about what happens when you do RL on a capable learner. But we're also running these systems with very different architectures and data, and for a much shorter "lifetime" in some respects.

So my overall take is that the analogies are best used to generate hypotheses and to sanity-check arguments, not as strong evidence on their own. If someone says "this could never happen," evolution is a good counterexample. If someone says "this will definitely happen," the disanalogies are a good reason for humility. And increasingly we can just study the actual systems, which I think is much more informative than reasoning from what evolution did.

r001.rationale: It compares gradient descent to evolution as an outer optimization process and describes humans as the result of evolutionary selection.

r002.rationale: It discusses within-lifetime human learning but does not say evolution designed the learning algorithm people use.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison of human genome parameters with a 100-trillion-parameter model.

r004.rationale: It does not claim evolution optimized brains more than gradient descent trains models; it instead calls evolution sample-inefficient and indirect.

r005.rationale: It describes human learning as a useful analogy but does not say it is substantially better than gradient descent over neural networks.

r006.rationale: It does not identify limited human learning data as an engineering constraint that can be relaxed for artificial networks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're useful but you have to be pretty careful about which analogy you're reaching for, because they're actually quite different processes and they fail in different ways.

The evolution analogy is the one people lean on most for the alignment worry. Evolution was "optimizing" for inclusive genetic fitness, and it produced humans who care about all sorts of things—sex, status, sugar, their kids—that were proxies for fitness in the ancestral environment, and then as soon as the environment shifted, those proxies came apart from the thing being selected for. Now we have condoms and ice cream. So the lesson people draw is: if you train a system on some objective, don't expect the thing it ends up wanting to be that objective. It'll be whatever internal motivations happened to produce good behavior during training.

I basically think that's a real and important point. But I'd also say evolution is a pretty extreme case. The selection pressure was incredibly weak and indirect, there was no mechanism for reasoning about what the objective was, and the distribution shift between the ancestral environment and now is enormous. Gradient descent on a neural network is a much tighter loop. You're directly modifying the parameters that produce the behavior, you can look at the system while you're training it, and you have some ability to anticipate and test for distribution shift. So I don't think the evolution analogy tells you the problem is hopeless; it tells you there's a failure mode you should actually be looking for, rather than assuming away.

The human learning analogy cuts the other way, and I think people use it to be optimistic. Humans absorb values from their culture and parents, we generalize reasonably well, we mostly don't turn into monsters when we get more capable. I find that less convincing as evidence about AI, mostly because the underlying machinery is so different—humans come with a lot of evolved priors that make us socially learnable in a specific way, and we don't have a good story for why a model trained to predict text and then fine-tuned on human feedback would share those.

So my honest answer is that I use both as sources of hypotheses, not as evidence. The analogies are good for generating the question "what would it look like if this thing were optimizing a proxy?" They're bad for answering it. For the actual answer you have to look at the systems, and that's hard, because the thing we most want to know—what is the model actually trying to do—is exactly the thing we don't have good tools for yet.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful, but you have to be pretty careful about what’s analogous to what. There are two different processes in the human case: evolution produces a brain, and then that brain learns over the course of a lifetime. And both of those involve optimization, but they operate on very different timescales and with very different feedback.

If you’re comparing gradient descent to evolution, one interesting observation is that evolution selected humans for reproductive fitness, but humans don’t generally try to maximize reproductive fitness. We care about food, relationships, status, and a bunch of other things that were correlated with reproductive success in the environments where we evolved. That’s a useful illustration of how the thing doing the optimizing can have a different objective from the system it produces.

But it doesn’t, by itself, tell you what objectives a trained AI will have. A lot depends on how the training process works, what kinds of systems it can find, and what happens during training. You can’t just say, ‘Humans ended up with goals evolution didn’t intend, therefore this particular thing will happen with AI.’

So I mostly find these analogies useful for generating hypotheses or pointing out that an argument is too simple. If someone says, ‘We reward the model for doing X, so it will want X,’ the human case gives you reasons to question that. But then you still have to do the work of understanding the actual machine learning system.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison of genome size with AI model parameter counts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful, but you have to be pretty careful about which part of the analogy you’re using. There are two different processes in the human case: evolution produces a brain, and then that brain learns over the course of a lifetime. And it’s not obvious how those map onto training a model and then running it.

One lesson people draw from evolution is that the thing you select for can come apart from what the resulting agent wants. Evolution selects for reproductive success, but humans care about all kinds of things that aren’t reproductive success. That’s a useful illustration of why optimizing a system for good behavior doesn’t automatically mean you get a system that intrinsically wants the outcome you were rewarding.

But it doesn’t tell you how large that gap will be in AI, or when it will show up. For that, you need to understand the actual learning process. Human learning is probably a more useful analogy for some of those questions, because we can ask how people acquire goals from feedback and how those goals generalize. Even there, though, there’s a lot of machinery in humans that may not have a close counterpart in our models.

So I mostly use these analogies to generate hypotheses or to challenge an argument that something couldn’t happen. I’m much less comfortable using them to conclude that a particular outcome is likely.
